## The current release. Use this one.

Guardrails for desktop AI agents, in Swift. Secret redaction and SSRF policy for anything
that reads your screen and follows links. Zero external packages, MIT.

```swift
// Package.swift
.package(url: "https://github.com/dotcomjack/grux-guardrails.git", from: "0.7.0")
.product(name: "GruxGuardrails", package: "grux-guardrails")
// then, in your source
import GruxGuardrails
```

## No source change, and that is the point

`Sources/` is byte identical to 0.6.1. Verify it rather than believe it:

```sh
git diff --stat 0.6.1..0.6.2 -- Sources/    # prints nothing
```

This release exists because the documentation shipped INSIDE the 0.6.1 tag told readers to
install 0.6.0. A tag is immutable, and its README is vendored into every checkout that
resolves it, so the release page a stranger reads and the copy in their `.build` directory
both carried the wrong instruction. Correcting the default branch fixed neither. A fix on a
branch is not a fix in a tag.

The structural half matters more than the correction: **the version now moves in the same
commit that gets tagged**, so a tag's own documentation names the tag it lives in. Bumping
after tagging would have reproduced the bug one release later.

## The other corrections, all documentation

- **The published bare 40-character credential leak rate was wrong by roughly 50%.** It read
  "roughly 1.3%" in three files. That is the pre-0.5.0 figure: 0.5.0 took the rate to 0.875%
  and updated the CHANGELOG and nothing else, so the number was stale for three releases.
  Measured across 8 runs on three machines it is 0.78% to 0.97%, so roughly 0.85%.
- **The guard on that rate is looser than this project's own rule asks for, and now says so.**
  It trips at 2.0%. At 20,000 trials the sampling deviation is about 0.065 points, so 2.0
  sits roughly 18 deviations above the mean and the rate could more than double before it
  fires. It is left where it is and recorded as a known gap, because moving a published
  threshold in either direction changes the claim the library makes.
- **The threat model said "two pure functions".** The public API is five: `redact`,
  `evaluate`, two `wrapAsUntrusted` overloads and `newFenceID`. A threat model naming two
  entry points invites a reviewer to review two.
- **`docs/CORPUS.md` gained a provenance column**, separating numbers a test recomputes on
  every run from numbers measured once against corpora that are not in this repository.
  Three rows cited a test that structurally could not produce the number beside it.
- **The install-snippet coherence test now checks the README's primary snippet.** It had
  required a code block to contain `let package = Package(`, so the one-line form was never
  checked. It now selects fenced Swift blocks by content rather than by line number.

Full detail in [CHANGELOG.md](https://github.com/dotcomjack/grux/blob/main/CHANGELOG.md).

## Still true, and worth repeating on every release

Six tags before 0.5.0 leak credentials and are left resolvable on purpose, documented in
[docs/DISCLOSURE-2026-08.md](https://github.com/dotcomjack/grux/blob/main/docs/DISCLOSURE-2026-08.md).
The failure was that the library failed to redact ITS USERS' secrets. No credential
belonging to the author has ever been in this repository.
